To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we can formally state sufficient conditions such that, if a protocol model is secure, then a more detailed model taking into account data encoding is secure too.

(i) the encoding and decoding operations can be safely abstracted away in formal security protocol model extraction and verification, and (ii) they can also be safely abstracted in formal protocol model-based code generation.

we have formally stated sufficient conditions, checka-ble on sequential code, for a protocol model to be secure under a Dolen-Yao adversary, even if the encoding and decoding transformations of the protocol are implemented in a non-trivial way.
In summary, our research is concerned with
providing a formal framework for the design of secure data encoding and decoding operations.
the problem of how to safely abstract away data encoding/decoding in the context of formal security protocol modeling and analysis.
the problem of how to formally reason about data encoding and decoding operations when using formal methods for security protocols analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
if an abstract model is secure, then any concrete implementation of the encoding/encoding operations is implied to be as secure as the abstract one.
the security of a protocol model is not only a property of the protocol itself, but also of the data encodings and decodings it relies on.
, if the encoding/decodings of the abstract model are implemented in a way that satisfies the conditions, then the abstract protocol is secure and the refined model will be too.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proposed abstraction is safe for a wide class of implementations, and thus can be exploited by both model extraction and automated code generation methods, which are complementary to each other.
the paper presents a general method to formally verify the security of data encoding and decoding operations, in the context of formal methods for cryptographic protocol analysis.
we provide the means to safely abstract away encoding/decoding transformations when formally modeling security protocols.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of abstract models is not necessarily a weakness, as long as the abstract model satisfies certain properties that can be checked on code, and the encoding/decryption operations are implemented accordingly.
, when using formal methods to verify security protocols, one should not forget to consider the impact of encoding/decoding transformations.
it is possible to reason about security protocols without being forced to make assumptions on the encoding and decoding operations that are too specific to a given implementation.
